title: Mapped peat of Indonesia on the 0.01 degree grid
key: row = floor((lat + 90) / 0.01 + 1e-7), column = floor((lon + 180) / 0.01 + 1e-7), cell = row * 36000 + column; the centre of a cell is ((row + 0.5) * 0.01 - 90, (column + 0.5) * 0.01 - 180).
rule: A cell of 0.01 degree (about 1.1 km) is in the mask when its centre lies inside a polygon of the peat map; a place is "on mapped peat" when the cell it falls in is in the mask.
limitation: The test is made at the centre of a 0.01 degree cell, on a map drawn at 1:250,000 and downloaded with a generalisation of 0.002 degree (about 220 m), so a place near the edge of a peat area can be tagged wrongly. The map is the 2011 national map; it says where peat was mapped, not how deep it is or what state it is in.

source.title: National peat map of Indonesia
source.via_title: Indonesia peat lands (2012), ArcGIS item d52e0e67ad21401cbf3a2c002599cf58
source.license: No licence is stated for the Global Forest Watch copy: the licence field of its metadata and of the ArcGIS item is empty (checked 21 Nov 2026). The same national map (Ritung et al. 2011) is included in PEATMAP (Xu et al. 2018, University of Leeds, doi:10.5518/252), which is published under CC BY 4.0.

checks.grid: same cell and centre as vendor/second-sight/pipeline/data/grid.py on 372 points

encoding: "runs" is a flat list of pairs. Each pair is one run of neighbouring cells in a row: the first number is the cell number of the first cell minus that of the first cell of the run before (for the first run, the cell number itself), the second is how many cells the run has. Runs are in rising order and do not touch.
